newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Amoco, Shell combine Permian Basin operations.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Amoco, Shell combine Permian Basin operations.

text.p: Amoco Corp. and Shell Oil Co. have agreed to combine their operations in the historic Permian Basin oil and natural gas fields of west Texas and southeast New Mexico, the companies said Tuesday.
When it opens for business March 1, their Altura Energy Ltd. venture will be the nation's third largest U.S. independent oil producer and the largest producer in Texas, the companies said.

Amoco will own 64 percent and Shell 36 percent of the partnership company, which in 1996 had pro forma gross daily production from 6,300 wells of about 170,000 barrels of oil and 220 million cubic feet of natural gas.
The venture, which culminated two years of talks between the rival major oil companies, continued a trend of consolidation in a domestic oil industry seeking to cut costs to boost profits.

"I think it's consistent with the trend that has been ongoing," said Bud Tower, energy analyst with New Orleans investment firm Howard Weil Labouisse Friedrichs. "I cannot imagine this is the last of it we are going to see."

The Permian Basin holds the largest concentration of oil and natural gas reserves in the lower 48 U.S. states and has been in production since the first discoveries gushed out of the earth in 1921. After peaking at 2.1 million barrels per day in 1974, crude oil production in the basin has since fallen off to a little more than 1 million barrels per day.

"We've lost as an industry 50 percent of the production," Jim Posey, Altura's president said. "We cannot operate in isolation in the future like we have in the past, and we've got to find ways to partner with each other."
In recent years, area land offices have been as busy as the oil fields, with producers aggressively buying and selling leaseholdings in the basin in a bid to lower exploration and production costs.

"This (consolidation) has kept fields in production at higher levels than would have been true otherwise," said historian Roger Olien of the University of Texas-Permian Basin. "What they are doing is keeping the Permian Basin as a region producing longer by producing oil more efficiently."

Altura, Spanish for "height" or "summit", will be headquartered in Houston, with 280 employees here and another 650 workers in the oil and gas fields centered around Midland, Texas, the companies said.

"This is a great day for Altura, Amoco, Shell, and the Permian Basin," Posey said. "I truly believe we have established a solid foundation for this company that will -- as its name implies -- reach new heights in our industry."
The companies said they formed the venture seeking to reduce costs and increase the value of their exploration and production activities in the mature Permian Basin.

Shell Oil, a Houston-based unit of Anglo-Dutch Royal Dutch/Shell Group, and Chicago-based Amoco announced plans for the venture in October 1996. Talks on the venture stalled late last year, but Amoco executives in recent weeks signaled that a definitive agreement was imminent.
